title: The platypus lays eggs, has no stomach, and males carry venom in spurs on their hind feet
body: The platypus is one of only five living mammal species that lay eggs. A female lays two leathery eggs about **17 mm** long and, having no teats, feeds her young with milk that seeps from pores in her skin. Males have a venomous spur on each hind foot that can cause excruciating pain in humans. Its rubbery bill carries about 40,000 electroreceptors that sense the electric fields of its prey, it has no functional stomach, and it has ten sex chromosomes where most mammals have two. When the first pelt reached Britain in 1798, scientists suspected a hoax.

cover.alt: A platypus swimming at the surface of a green river, its broad rubbery bill and dense brown fur visible

slides.heading: Platypus: fact or myth?

items.text: Females feed their young through skin pores
It senses prey by their electric fields
It has a stomach like other mammals

slides.explanation: Only males keep the spur; females lose a vestigial sheath as they mature. Adults grind food with keratinised pads and lack a functional stomach.

slides.question: How many electroreceptors does a platypus bill carry?
slides.explanation: About 40,000, arranged in rows along the bill, alongside touch-sensing mechanoreceptors. They pick up the electric fields produced by the muscles of its prey.

slides.heading: Sex chromosomes
slides.note: Humans have two, XX or XY; the platypus has ten

slides.alt: A round nest of dried leaves with two small oval platypus eggs at its centre, displayed in a museum
slides.caption: A platypus nest with two eggs, displayed at the MUSE science museum in Trento. The eggs are about 17 mm long and hatch after roughly ten days of incubation.

slides.heading: A hoax with scissors
slides.text: When Captain John Hunter sent a pelt and a sketch to Britain in 1798, scientists suspected a joke. In his 1799 description George Shaw wrote that it was impossible not to doubt its genuine nature, and he reportedly took scissors to the pelt to look for stitches holding a duck's beak onto a beaver-like body.

slides.label: the year William Hay Caldwell confirmed that the platypus lays eggs
slides.text: European naturalists had doubted the reports of egg-laying for most of a century. The eggs develop inside the mother for about 28 days, then incubate outside for about 10.
